text: Knowing that purple teaming is deliberately collaborative is one thing. Actually running a session that produces real improvement is another. This lesson walks through the real structure of a purple team exercise, from the planning that happens before anyone executes a technique, through to the moment a gap gets found and fixed in the room.

It starts well before the session opens. The team picks a short, prioritized list of specific techniques, usually driven by real threat intelligence — a ransomware group's known behavior, a technique seen in a recent incident, or a gap flagged by an earlier red team report. Every technique gets a defined success criterion, and someone is assigned to facilitate and scribe, because the entire value of the exercise depends on an accurate, real-time record of what happened.

Inside the session, red doesn't run a stealthy multi-stage attack chain. Red announces one specific technique, names it, and executes it right then at a known timestamp, while blue is already watching the SIEM and EDR console live. Within seconds, the whole room finds out together whether anything fired, and the result — detected or not, how fast, how clean — gets logged immediately.

When a technique doesn't trigger an alert, that's not a failure — it's the exercise doing exactly what it's for. Red and blue immediately ask why, together: is the right log source even being collected? Does a rule exist but check the wrong field? Is a threshold tuned so high this behavior slides under it? Blue tunes or writes a fix on the spot, and then red re-runs the exact same technique to confirm it actually works before anyone moves on. Skipping that re-run is the most common way these exercises quietly fail to produce real change.

A real session might cover a dozen or more techniques in a day. The scribe's tracker captures technique ID, timestamp, detection status, time-to-detect, and a named owner for anything left open, and the facilitator keeps the room from getting stuck debugging one stubborn gap for the whole session. Nothing unresolved waits for a report nobody reads — it gets an owner and a deadline instead.

Running the exercise well depends on both sides speaking the same language about exactly which technique just happened. Next lesson covers how that shared vocabulary works in practice — mapping every single action, live, to its real MITRE ATT&CK tactic and technique ID.
